newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarke and George meet...maybe for last time.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarke and George meet...maybe for last time.

text.p: Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George met in the midlands city of Nottingham on Thursday to discuss British interest rates for what could be the last time.
Clarke's election campaign commitments meant the meeting was held on his own turf, and outside London for the first time.

With no-one expecting rates to rise just three weeks before May Day elections, it looks like George was condemned to a 250-mile round trip for little return -- apart from possible farewells with his monetary other half.

Despite making some headway with attacks on the opposition Labour Party's policies over privatisation and trade unions, the ruling Conservatives still trail by 15 points or more in opinion polls. That would translate into a Labour landslide and give shadow Chancellor Gordon Brown the keys to the Treasury.

But Clarke would not hear of suggestions that this was his last crack of the monetary whip. Instead he told reporters that all Britons were now better off and took the opportunity again to attack what he called Labour's privatisation U-turn.

Labour has said it will consider selling off Britain's air traffic control service to help balance the books. "They are treating the electorate with complete contempt if they deny they have had a total and utter change of mind," the ever-ebullient Clarke said.

George arrived at the Inland Revenue offices flanked by his deputy governor, Howard Davies, and chief economist, Mervyn King. Economists said they would have argued for base rates to rise to 6.25 percent from six, as they have throughout this year -- but to no avail.

Clarke is far too political to stick rates up, and therefore put pressure on home loan rates to rise, with elections looming. "The chance of a rate rise today is as close to zero as any event could conceivably be," said Yamaichi chief economist John Shepperd.
Clarke arrived, resplendent in a blue rosette. He said he had been campaigning in his local Rushcliffe constituency in the leafy suburbs of Nottingham.
But local reporters were confused as to why George had been dragged so far from the Bank's Threadneedle Street home in London.

Clarke, with a nearly 20,000 majority, perhaps does not have to try too hard to secure his re-election. "He's loved and hated in equal measure around here. But largely loved in his constituency," the reporter said.

But that still leaves the question of why the Bank took all three of their heavyweights so far to argue for what they must know they won't get. Economists said it was to put a marker down for the first meetings after the elections.

"George will simply be rehearsing the arguments that in the coming months he will put before a new audience, one which is likely to prove more receptive to his policy demands," said UBS economist Alex Garrard.

After 18 years in opposition, Labour is desperate to show it is not the same party which allowed inflation and spending to soar in the 1970s. Brown may take an early opportunity to establish his anti-inflation credentials by hiking base rates.
He has also pledged to overhaul the whole monetary framework and replace it with a broader committee. So, Thursday could have been the end of an era, of a sort, for George too.
So was a tear shed across the monetary table? No-one was saying, but a Treasury official said Ken and Eddie had always got on well. "They often sat around chatting away at the meetings."
With that one phrase, she exploded a long held market myth. Each month, the monetary meeting is assiduously timed on the basis that a long meeting could signal disagreement over policy.
"We've often laughed about that," the official said.
